docs.title: Trump’s tariffs put a spotlight on forced labour. It isn’t going away.
docs.text:
Global 
 Trump’s tariffs put a spotlight on forced labour. It isn’t going away.
 Richard Vanderford , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 8 Oct 2026, 06:55 AM IST 
 Summary
 ​The president’s use of forced-labor concerns to resurrect his tariffs faces a Democratic-led legal challenge, but America’s trade partners are toughening up their own laws either way. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Trump administration resurrected its global tariffs by shining a light on forced labor. The tariffs face a court challenge, but the spotlight isn’t going away.
 After the U.S. Supreme Court in February shot down President Trump’s global tariffs—which relied on emergency economic powers—the administration turned to a new theory to partially revive them, accusing America’s trade partners of failing to take action against forced labor.
 Critics of the novel theory, including Democratic attorneys general and governors in more than two dozen states, last week asked a New York-based federal court to invalidate the new tariffs. The Trump administration turned to forced labor as a pretext, they argued.
 The White House didn’t respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.
 Regardless of the administration’s motivations, after the U.S. unveiled its forced-labor tariffs, a number of U.S. trading partners began to beef up their own legal regimes. Increased global scrutiny on supply chains is likely to continue no matter what the U.S. Court of International Trade decides.
 “It’s a big issue,” said Luis Lozano, the former president of Toyota’s Mexico unit and who now serves as chief executive of Mexico City-based advisory Odysseus Business Intelligence.
 “There’s more eyes,” Lozano said. “And there’s certain words as a global company you don’t want combined with your brand. One is ‘forced labor.’”
 Firm line
 Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, under which the Trump administration has imposed its new round of tariffs, lets the president take action against countries it finds have engaged in unfair trade practices. Various administrations have regularly used it over trade disputes in a number of sectors, from beer to green technology.
 The Trump administration supercharged the use of this legal power by taking action in July against 60 economies that it said had failed to adequately address forced labor, putting competing U.S. workers on an unfair footing.
 The U.S. has for decades taken a much firmer line on forced labor than its peer countries, first banning imports tied to the practice in 1930.
 In 2022, a tough measure specifically targeting China came into force. The Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act effectively bans the import of any goods that can be tied to Xinjiang over human-rights concerns. Beijing has denied allegations of forced labor and other abuses in the region.
 That law forced many businesses to investigate their supply chains. Automaker Volkswagen, for example, in 2024 had a shipment of vehicles kept out of the U.S. after finding a single part traced to Xinjiang. VW said at the time it diligently investigates possible human-rights issues in its supply chains.
 As of August, the U.S. had under the UFLPA investigated about 44,000 shipments and denied entry to nearly 27,000 of those, most of them electronics.
 Mixed records
 Many U.S. allies have had more mixed records on forced labor. The European Union is planning to enforce its forced-labor import ban by December 2027, nearly a century after the first U.S. law was passed.
 Canada agreed to bar imports of goods made with forced labor as part of a free-trade agreement from Trump’s first term. But as of Oct. 2, Canada had held up just 53 shipments for inspection over forced-labor concerns and blocked two, one of textiles and another of seafood, according to figures provided by the Canada Border Services Agency.
 Canada is one of the countries that have scrambled to bulk up their forced-labor enforcement amid the U.S. push. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government proposed a tougher forced-labor law in June, about a week after the USTR filed a preliminary report that criticized the forced-labor records of Canada and other U.S. trading partners.
 “Regardless of whether one is for or against the tariffs, everyone has to admit that the 301 investigations have ignited conversations about forced labor in supply chains all over the world,” said Laura Murphy, a forced-labor researcher who advised the Biden administration.
 “In some places where advocates have been arguing for new action for a decade, we are seeing sudden movement,” Murphy said.
 Shot in the arm
 The administration’s focus on forced labor is a welcome one, said Samir Goswami, director of forced-labor programs at Hague-based Global Rights Compliance, which works with governments and international institutions to promote international law.
 “We just needed to see enforcement through any instrument,” Goswami said.
 Colombia, for example, in late September banned the import of goods with any forced-labor touchpoint. India did the same in July.
 The USTR in September said it had brought 50 countries together for training on imposing and enforcing forced-labor bans. Mexico and Argentina committed on the sidelines of a G-20 meeting last week to work to eliminate forced labor from global supply chains.
 Countries around the world are unlikely to reverse their new forced-labor-related policy moves regardless of what the U.S. court decides, said Richard Mojica, head of the customs-and-import-trade practice at the law firm Miller & Chevalier.
 “Countries that have gone through this are unlikely to wind down any of these laws,” said Mojica, who advises large international businesses.

Global 
 What six years of inflation mean for the midterms
 Owen Tucker-Smith , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 8 Oct 2026, 06:42 AM IST 
 Summary
 Inflation is cooler than it was four years ago, but voters are still paying much higher prices. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Four years ago, in the run-up to the last midterm elections, prices were rising more than twice as quickly as they are now. President Trump has repeatedly reminded voters of the 2022 inflation rate, blaming high prices on his predecessor.
 But Americans, weary from six years of quickly rising prices that have eaten away at their paychecks, might blame Republicans anyway as they head to the polls next month.
 Inflation sits at about 3.4%, far lower than its recent peak in 2022, when it topped 9%. Yet that means prices are still rising, adding to the higher costs consumers have absorbed in previous years. All kinds of everyday goods are 30% more expensive than they were in 2020. The prices of new cars, child care, beef and paper towels have all soared.
 Economists say that consumers generally focus more on the cumulative effect of years of steadily rising prices than on individual monthly metrics, and that it takes years for consumers to adjust to new price baselines. That helps explain why voters might be aggravated and still surprised when they see, for example, a $5 price tag on a gallon of milk.
 Prices for some items, like eggs, butter and cheese, have fallen over the past year. But newer signs of pricing pressure have emerged: Gas prices have lurched higher in recent months. Mortgage rates that have pushed past 7% and record home prices have shattered the playbook for buying a new home.
 “Voters have become incredibly impatient and disconcerted” by inflation, said Stephen Weymouth, a professor at Georgetown University’s business school who has studied the impact of inflation on elections.
 Slowing wage growth
 Over the past six years, prices have, on average, risen faster than wages.
 A swath of the population simply didn’t receive wage hikes to match the pace of inflation, which has eroded Americans’ purchasing power and likely contributed to an overall souring mood. The trend has been pronounced recently: In both July and August, inflation outpaced average hourly wage growth.
 Many employers have given raises that match inflation. But those raises don’t necessarily lead to happier consumers.
 When they give raises, bosses tend to tell staff that “you’ve done a great job at work and I’m rewarding you,” said Neale Mahoney, an economics professor at Stanford University. “So when you go to the grocery store and you see the price increase eroding away those wage gains, you see it as something being done to you.”
 Age of inflation
 Overall prices, as measured by the consumer-price index, have risen almost 29% in the past six years. During the six years before that, prices crept up at a third of that pace.
 Since the pandemic, prices have leapt in all corners of the economy: coffee, cleaning products, streaming services, hardware. A Hulu no-ads subscription jumped from around $12 to more than $20 and a New York City subway fare hit $3. The USPS “forever stamp” cost 55 cents in 2020. It has risen 49% to 82 cents.
 Big-ticket items
 Inflation data usually doesn’t include some of the expenses people care about most. U.S. out-of-pocket spending on healthcare per capita rose roughly 47% between 2020 and 2026.
 The cost of borrowing money also keeps climbing. Prices of housing, daycare and preschool, car maintenance and pet services have all grown more over the past six years than average hourly wages.
 Meanwhile, Americans have found themselves saddled with ballooning debt, further blunting the impact of income growth. A recent report by Century Foundation, a progressive think tank, found that in recent years, more than half of workers’ raises have gone toward debt payments.
 Strong spending, sinking confidence
 American consumers are spending big, and household spending has grown faster over the past 12 months as of August than it did last year. The S&P 500 is up 14% this year and the unemployment rate is low.
 So consumers might have a pretty good view of the economy—if it weren’t for the stubborn inflation squeezing their disposable incomes.
 While economists keep a close eye on the year-over-year inflation rate, consumers often compare prices they see at the store to benchmarks stuck in their head from years ago.
 And many consumers, when recalling what they believe they paid for a product a year ago, think they paid less than they actually did, said Michael Weber, an economist at Purdue University. They also notice price increases much more than they notice price cuts, said Weber.
 This might help explain why consumer sentiment dropped last month, according to the University of Michigan’s survey; sentiment among Republicans has fallen 20% since the start of the year.
 Impact on the midterms
 Inflation often punishes incumbents. In 2022 and 2024, high prices were the Democrats’ Achilles’ heel.
 Now, a president who made inflation a centerpiece of his political comeback is being asked to answer for the fact that on average, it costs around $50,000 to buy a car and around $60 to fill its tank with gas.
 It is easy for voters to connect the dots between Trump’s policies and high prices, Weymouth said. Consumers watched the prices of goods like bananas rise after the onset of reciprocal tariffs, Mahoney noted, and fall only slightly after those tariffs were rescinded.
 In a recent Wall Street Journal poll, 60% of respondents said Trump’s policies had made the economy worse.
 A White House spokeswoman said that the president had cut the cost of prescription drugs and added more than a million private-sector jobs to the economy.
 “The Democrats and Joe Biden destroyed our economy and crushed American families, and

 Ramita Mishra , Dhirendra Kumar 4 min read 8 Oct 2026, 05:50 AM IST 
 Summary
 Colombia is eyeing enhanced law-enforcement cooperation with India to combat drug trafficking, focusing on drone shield technology from Bharat Electronics Ltd

 New Delhi: Colombia is seeking deeper law-enforcement cooperation with India to counter drug-trafficking, and procuring drone shield technology from state-run Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL) as the South American country looks to strengthen its fight against drug cartels and narco-terrorists. 
 The Colombian government is also considering creating a new position of police-attaché at its embassy in New Delhi, Colombia’s ambassador to India, Victor Hugo Echeverri Jaramillo said in an interview.
 “I think we face common threats. Sometimes you think that the international problem of drugs relies only on Colombia, but in fact, the reality is that it is an international problem; there are networks, no boundaries. They are transnational, they work as a multinational corporation. So the only way to face it is through international cooperation,” said Jaramillo. 
 “The Colombian police can share information very swiftly with the local police when it is needed to tackle international crime . India is a transit (for the drugs) to go to Australia, to New Zealand,” he added.
 A senior Indian government official requesting anonymity said Indian agencies have seized cocaine originating from Colombia but have not come across any case in which there was evidence that the consignments were being routed through India to Australia or New Zealand. 
 From drug lord Pablo Escobar to the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC) or Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, the country has had a violent past. India, meanwhile, has declared all districts free of Left Wing Extremism (LWE)-related violence, according to a 1 August government statement. 
 Jaramillo said the cooperation arrangement between the police forces focuses on intelligence and technology. 
 “I think it's very focused with some very specific samples on intelligence—artificial intelligence—because this is not a regular confrontation. When you have this kind of confrontation, where there is a group that is hidden in the jungle, in the case of Colombia, they are producing drugs, and you have to find them. Yes, you use technology. They are guerrillas if you still want to call them. They hit and hide. The territory is very big. Half of the country of Colombia could be empty. A very important part of that is intelligence technology,” said Jaramillo. 
 He added that the Colombian government is in talks with BEL to procure drone-shield technology.
 A Colombian delegation had visited BEL‘s Ghaziabad Unit and Central Research Laboratory-Ghaziabad in March 2026. 
 “There has been an interest that Colombia has been exploring. And we have been in contact with India because part of our challenges in Colombia is fighting these drug cartels, terrorists, narco-terrorists… They (BEL) have this facility in Ghaziabad. Very competitive prices. When you compare prices, you can get an anti-drone shield in India compared to the European competitors. It happened during the previous government,” Jaramillo said. 
 Queries emailed to the spokespersons of National Police of Colombia, and India’s ministry of external affairs, and BEL on 29 September remained unanswered till press time. 
 Queries emailed on 6 October to narcotics control bureau director general, and spokespersons for the ministry of home affairs and Interpol also remained unanswered till press time. 
 Colombia’s ministry of national defense in an email response said that it has assigned Mint’s query to the Colombian National Police and added, “The ministry of national defense is committed to improving the citizen experience regarding procedures and services within the Defense Sector.”
 Building links 
 The two countries have already begun limited cooperation on police training. Twenty-five Colombian police officers from the National Police of Colombia attended an Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (Itec) course on artificial intelligence for human security at Rashtriya Raksha University in Gujarat from 26 March to 8 April 2025. 
 “At present, no additional training programme or visit by officers of the National Police of Colombia has been scheduled. To date, Rashtriya Raksha University has not conducted a similar training programme for officers from other Latin American countries,” said Ankit Kumar, director, School of International Cooperation, Security and Strategic Languages, Rashtriya Raksha University, in an emailed response. 
 Indian security experts said the India-Colombia partnership could complement each other's strengths. 
 Dependra Pathak, retired special commissioner of police, Delhi Police, said India’s experience in dealing with narcotics and insurgency along its borders, along with BEL’s capabilities in drone technology, could complement Colombia’s expertise in combating drug cartels. 
 “It is going to complement each other's strength—India's advancement in technical training in the field of artificial intelligence and IT on the one hand—and our public sector undertaking defence manufacturing strength that is Bharat Electronics particularly in the field of drones," said Dependra Pathak, retired special commissioner of police, Delhi Police.
 Strategic experts said this collaboration enhances India’s status as a global defence tech provider. “Hosting foreign police forces portends India’s technological advancement in defense and surveillance. Secondly, physical interaction with Colombian officials gives Indian agencies knowledge of how Colombia has dealt with cross-border crime, drug cartels, and urban conflicts,” said Aprajita Kashyap,

 Ahead of midterms that could turn on high prices and borrowing costs, the secretary dresses down officials.

 WASHINGTON—Scott Bessent was fuming.
 President Trump had just asked his Treasury secretary to investigate allegations of fraud in Minnesota’s Somali community—and Bessent thought one of his top deputies was dragging his feet.
 During a January meeting at the Treasury Department, Bessent confronted John Hurley, the agency’s undersecretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, yelling at him in front of aides and unleashing profanities. Bessent shouted so loudly that staff working nearby could hear him, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
 Weeks later, Bessent discussed with aides the idea of finding Hurley, who had been confirmed by the Senate for his position, a job outside the department, the people said. Hurley left to be U.S. ambassador to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. It was one of a string of high-level departures in the top ranks of the department at a moment when the Treasury secretary was staring down the biggest challenges of his career.
 Bessent’s behavior was a factor—and sometimes the most-important one—in the departure of multiple key officials, people familiar with the matter said.
 Since he became Treasury secretary in early 2025, Bessent has dressed down senior advisers and junior staffers alike over issues large and small, according to more than a dozen current and former Treasury officials.
 But Trump has only pulled Bessent closer, empowering him to solve stubborn problems in the economy, including higher borrowing costs, intractable inflation pushed up by gas prices and government debt that is piling up quickly. At the same time, Bessent has been tasked with ending the war in Iran with a sweeping sanctions plan.
 A senior administration official who worked with Bessent said the president’s entire economic policy agenda is on the Treasury secretary’s shoulders. “Scott cannot fail,” the official said.
 His backers say his hard-charging style gets results. But 20 months into his tenure at the department, Bessent is facing skepticism on Wall Street and an economy that could wreck Republican chances in November’s midterm elections.
 Bessent advised Trump to pursue a “3-3-3” policy: cutting the budget deficit to 3% of gross domestic product by 2028, spurring GDP growth of 3% and producing an additional three million barrels of oil a day. But growth has been around 2%, and oil production has increased less than a million barrels a day since Trump took office. The budget deficit is now over 6% of GDP, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. U.S. debt overall recently topped $40 trillion.
 A deepening selloff in U.S. government bonds has driven the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note to highs last seen more than two decades ago, despite a stepped-up buyback program Bessent set into motion to contain the increase. The result is higher borrowing costs for Americans, a perilous trend for Republicans.
 The Iran war, meanwhile, has no clear end in sight, although there are signs the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and economic squeeze engineered by the Trump administration is making the regime more desperate for a way out. But the president recently rejected Iran’s offer for a deal and has also told aides he expects another U.S. bombing campaign against Iran after the midterms.
 Bessent, meanwhile, has projected unwavering confidence. He has dismissed his critics as “Bloomberg terminal bros,” referring to those on Wall Street questioning his moves, and quipped in a recent interview, “I am the house now,” citing the insights he has gained as Treasury secretary. “You can bet against me if you want.”
 He has become increasingly emboldened, making unilateral decisions that have confounded even some of his longtime allies and friends.
 And his temper has flared. He has shouted at staff for not moving fast enough to implement his ideas and for failing to combat unfavorable media coverage, some of the officials said. Last year, Bessent got so angry about the way his daily briefing book was organized that he picked up the binder full of papers and threw it at a wall, people familiar with the matter said.
 Bessent denied the account to The Wall Street Journal.
 “A lot of people in the investment community had hoped he was the adult in the room,” said Stephen Myrow, a former Treasury official and managing partner at Beacon Policy Advisors. Investors are “starting to see him as acting more and more like Trump…and that’s shaking confidence in him.”

 Hurley said in a statement that he was aligned with Bessent on the Minnesota fraud probe. “Scott Bessent is a brilliant and fearless warrior for President Trump and the American people,” he said.

 The silent electronic battleground shaping the future of warfare
 Alistair MacDonald , The Wall Street Journal 8 min read 7 Oct 2026, 06:42 AM IST 
 Summary
 From spoofing hypersonic missiles to jamming drone signals, combat zones are in the grip of an electronic arms race. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 KYIV, Ukraine—Earlier this year, two Russian ballistic missiles hurtled at hypersonic speeds toward a key government site in Ukraine’s capital city. They crashed into the Dnipro River after being intercepted by a radio signal.
 Around that time, the navigation apps on many phones in Kyiv showed users as located in Peru. It was the electronic calling card of Night Watch, an elite Ukrainian jamming unit that says it downed the missiles with its Lima system.
 A silent electronic battle is raging at the heart of the Russia-Ukraine war. Both sides are attacking and defending communication signals on an unprecedented scale, innovating at pace, while the U.S. and other Western countries are working to catch up. The Pentagon is investing heavily in new capabilities.
 “This is a new era of spectrum warfare,” said Lt. Col. Matt Sherburne, the U.S. Army’s chief for electronic warfare capabilities development.
 Electronic warfare isn’t new, but it fell out of focus in the West after the end of the Cold War. Then came Russia’s war on Ukraine, where swarms of drones have become the dominant weapon on the front lines. Both sides are now engaged in a constant game of cat and mouse, jumping around the frequency spectrum to jam and avoid each other, and they are increasingly using AI to do that.
 Electronic warfare is already reshaping the battlefield. The U.S. began its operation to grab former President Nicolás Maduro by using electronic warfare to knock out the ability of the Venezuelans to see and communicate. The Iran war saw the first deployment of the U.S.’s new signal-jamming jet, the EA-37B Compass Call.
 Also known as spectrum warfare, EW essentially relies on finding or disrupting the frequencies that adversaries are using, or hiding signals from enemy interference. At its simplest, that works by blasting signals to drown out, confuse or supplant an adversary’s communications.
 Ukraine’s Night Watch division uses Lima to blast signals over a 120-mile range that disrupt drones, missiles and guided bombs, said a major in the unit, known by his call sign Alchemist. The unit used Lima to confuse the ballistic missiles that crashed into the Dnipro, filling the air with false signals—a technique known as spoofing.
 Last November, Night Watch claimed one of its biggest scalps when it intercepted a hypersonic Kinzhal missile, once dubbed invincible by Russian President Vladimir Putin. Lima beamed a false navigation signal at the missile, prompting it to alter direction and break up under the pressure of its own extreme speed, according to Night Watch officers.
 Ukraine won’t say how often electronic warfare, rather than in-flight failure, is responsible for downing missiles and drones. It can be hard to tell the difference. Electronic interference can unintentionally divert a target to civilian areas.
 ​Ukrainian officers say that Lima can sometimes interfere with their own drones amid operations.
 Still, they are in no doubt of how effective electronic warfare is. One officer for Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said it suppresses 70% to 95% or radio-controlled drones detected in the sector where his team operates.
 Phantom Defense, a Ukrainian manufacturer, says that over the past year of operation, its systems detected more than 11,500 Russian drones, of which around 7,500 were successfully neutralized, with confirmed results via the video feeds from the drones, which the company also intercepts.
 And Ukraine is buying vast amounts, underscoring the success. Ukrainian firm December1 now sells thousands of its front-line and long-distance units a month, up from dozens in 2024.
 Ukrainian manufacturer Phantom Defense takes over the footage of Russian drones and intercepts them with electronic warfare.
 Since the start of the 20th century, when the British Royal Navy experimented with radio jamming and intercepting enemy communications, the vulnerability of radio signals has been exploited in combat. It truly took off in World War II, when the U.K. and Germany jammed and spoofed aerial navigation signals in what Winston Churchill dubbed the battle of the beams.
 As military communications and radar became more sophisticated during the Cold War, so did the technology to interfere with them.
 But in post-Cold War conflicts, the U.S. faced lower-tech adversaries in Afghanistan and Iraq. Further advances in electronic warfare were less of a priority for the Pentagon. U.S. officials say Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has been a wake-up call.
 Joshua Ransford never worried about electronic warfare when he served as a U.S. Marine in Iraq, because America’s adversaries had such little capability in this field. Later he joined the international legion of Ukraine’s armed forces in 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
 In his first days of fighting, Russian forces jammed his GPS signals and radio frequencies, rendering much of his equipment useless. The enemy flew drones that could find Ukrainian positions by sniffing out their electronic emissions, including radio.
 “It really sucked,” Ransford said.
 Today’s networked world offers jammers more targets than ever, from cellphones and satellite navigation systems to a plethora of new guided weapons and drones, as well as traditional radio and radar. By 2022, electronic warfare was one of the Pentagon’s top three procurement priorities, along with long-range munitions and affordable technology, for countering drones and missiles, according to Bill LaPlante, who was the Biden administration’s top procurement official.

docs.title: Stocks are riding high, bonds are wild—who wins in the end?
docs.text:
Global 
 Stocks are riding high, bonds are wild—who wins in the end?
 Martin Baccardax , Barrons 4 min read 8 Oct 2026, 06:24 AM IST 
 Summary
 A widening gap between stock and bond volatility gauges suggests equities could be overlooking inflation, borrowing, and interest-rate risks. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Stock and bond markets are telling very different stories about near-term risk.
 Stock investors want earnings growth, profit margin expansion, and smart capital spending. Bond investors want their money back, without inflation redoing its value, and not much else.
 But the two markets often look to each other for signals on the next big move, even if they’re focused on different catalysts. They typically don’t diverge much in their assessment of near-term risks.
 Today’s market, however, is different.
 The stock market’s go-to gauge of near-term volatility, the Cboe Global Markets’ Cboe Volatility Index, is hovering near its lowest levels of the year. It’s tumbled nearly 50% since concerns about the U.S.-Iran war—and the resulting oil price spike—peaked in late March.
 The VIX was last quoted at 15.67 points, and has closed above of the 20-point mark—a level typically associated with elevated, but not extreme, volatility—on only three trading days in the past five months.
 The bond market equivalent, the Merrill Lynch Options Volatility Estimate, tells a very different story. Better known a the MOVE Index, it’s risen nearly 43% since the start of the year and is just a few ticks shy of its late-March high of 107.67 points.
 Meanwhile, the gap between the two has widened to its largest since the Liberation Day tariff turmoil in April of last year.
 “The gauge everyone consults for risk is measuring the market where, for the moment, there is very little of it,” said Michael Gayed, portfolio manager of The Free Markets ETF. “While the market where the risk actually lives moves 40 basis points in a single month.”
 Stocks, of course, have resumed their late-spring rally, with the S&P 500 rising nearly 2% over the past month to a record closing high of 7818.93 points on Tuesday.
 But the bond market remains in turmoil, with 10-year Treasury yields rising to their highest level since 2002 at 5.35% on Tuesday, up some 58 basis points over the past month. Longer dated 30-year bonds, meanwhile, have jumped 48 basis points to a mutidecade high of 5.723%.
 Henry Allen, macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, says the volatility indexes are reflecting “two fundamentally different worlds.”
 “Over the last month, we’ve seen bond markets price in more inflation risk, more fiscal risk, and the risk of more restrictive policy rates,” he said. “But equities have generally brushed this off,” as they focus on the tech-led rally and the third-quarter earnings season.
 “In essence, we’re pricing the symptoms of a new regime (such as yields at multi-decade highs and wider sovereign bond spreads), without pricing the logical consequences” for other markets, he added.
 Last week’s trading action in the wake of the September jobs report seemed to underscore those two realities. Stocks powered higher after the softer-than-expected reading lowered Federal Reserve rate forecasts, but bond yields continued to rise nonetheless.
 “Equities priced a Fed that cuts, [long dated bonds] priced a government that keeps borrowing, and the two trades now sit in the same portfolio pointing in opposite directions,” said Gayed.
 Earnings might tell us which direction the market will follow. LSEG data suggested third-quarter S&P 500 profits will rise more than 30% from last year to more than $770 billion, with a tally topping $800 billion expected over the three months ending in December.
 Tech and the AI investment boom will drive nearly half of those gains, however, leaving the market increasingly reliant on just a few stocks to power its recent gains.
 Oil prices are back on the rise, as well, thanks to renewed hostilities in the Gulf region that have lifted Brent crude back above $102 a barrel, adding to inflation pressures and Fed rate hike bets.
 And broader risks from November’s midterm elections, now less than a month away, shouldn’t be ignored.
 Those risks make for a “worrisome” reading of the widening gap between the MOVE and VIX indexes, according to Saxo Bank’s investment and options strategist Koen Hoorelbeke.
 “Historically the MOVE precedes the VIX, but it takes a bit of time before the equity markets realize it’s not all roses and sunshine,” he said. “So, I expect volatility to rise (which is usually not a good thing for equities) in the coming months.”
 The gap between the two has been a useful indicator of late, with widening gaps in 2022 preceding a 20% stock market decline linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the massive spike in global oil prices, as well as the 9% pullback linked to the regional banking crisis the following year.
 “If there’s a lot of uncertainty in fixed income, it tends to bleed into the equity market too,” said Joe Mazzola, head trading and derivatives strategist at Schwab. “I wouldn’t say it’s a perfect indicator, but it needs to be seen as a tool in context with the broader market.”
 With risks piling up as year-end approaches, investors need to deploy as many tools as they can to manage risk.

 Mexico’s Sheinbaum is getting fed up with playing nice with the US
 Santiago Pérez , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 7 Oct 2026, 06:38 AM IST 
 Summary
 U.S. sanctions on alleged cartel-linked officials infuriate the president as she faces relentless pressure from the Trump administration. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 MEXICO CITY—President Claudia Sheinbaum began her workday at dawn last week by grilling Mexico’s top security and intelligence officials. She wasn’t happy.
 Inside the ornate National Palace, Sheinbaum confronted some of her most trusted aides over their plans to freeze the local bank accounts of former Mexican officials linked to a state governor from Sheinbaum’s ruling party. The U.S. Treasury was about to target those former officials with sanctions for allegedly accepting bribes to protect the Sinaloa cartel’s drug-smuggling operations, said people familiar with the discussion.
 To Sheinbaum, her security chiefs were going beyond the close cooperation with American law enforcement that has been the hallmark of her two-year tenure by taking for granted that the U.S. had solid evidence linking the former officials to drug cartels, these people said.
 She was unusually harsh with Security Minister Omar García Harfuch, a confidant who has guided her policies throughout her political career, the people said. Sheinbaum said that the U.S. measures were part of an effort to destabilize Mexico and her government, they added.
 In the end, Sheinbaum consented to freeze the former officials’ accounts. Refusing to do so would have likely strained relations with the U.S.
 Spokespersons for Sheinbaum and García Harfuch declined to comment.
 The episode reflects the harsher tone that Sheinbaum is taking toward American efforts to fight drug trafficking on her country’s soil and the Trump administration’s targeting of her leftist party, Morena. In recent weeks, Sheinbaum has criticized the U.S. at mass rallies and public events, blaming the northern neighbor’s insatiable demand for narcotics and defending Mexican sovereignty as President Trump has repeatedly said that Mexico is run by cartels.
 “We Mexicans don’t want interference, interventionism, or violations of our territorial integrity,” she said before tens of thousands of supporters in Mexico City’s central Zócalo square late last month. She has also confronted state governors from opposition parties who want to strengthen security cooperation with the U.S.
 Sheinbaum is facing immense pressure at home and abroad to deliver results in the fight against drug cartels while more ruling party officials face corruption allegations, said Alberto Capella, who served as security chief of Tijuana and the states of Morelos and Quintana Roo.
 “Collaboration with the U.S. is a prerequisite for achieving results; when that collaboration is restricted or denied, it renders your work meaningless,” Capella said. He added that security officials face rising domestic political pressure to back off from corruption scandals.
 Morena leader Ariadna Montiel has said that there is no room for corruption within the party, while adding that certain allegations of corruption aim to undermine Mexico’s sovereignty.
 Last week, the U.S. Treasury imposed sanctions on 21 individuals with alleged links to the Sinaloa cartel, including officials who allegedly accepted bribes to protect the criminal group at border crossings in the cities of Tijuana and Mexicali. At the center of the alleged scheme was the then-husband of Marina del Pilar Ávila, the governor of the border state of Baja California.
 The State Department said that the sanctions “highlight the corrosive reach of cartel influence into Mexican governance, particularly in Baja California.”
 The sanctions were the latest in a string of corruption allegations rocking Morena in recent months. The Trump administration has also indicted the governor of western Sinaloa state and revoked the U.S. visa of a son of former nationalist President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, Sheinbaum’s mentor and predecessor.
 Sheinbaum criticized past Treasury sanctions against three Mexican financial institutions over money-laundering allegations. Although Mexican authorities detected irregularities in some accounts managed by the firms, they found no evidence establishing links to criminal organizations, Sheinbaum said last week.
 The companies denied wrongdoing. Sheinbaum’s administration took over the three financial institutions last year to prevent a run on deposits.
 Sheinbaum has decried the lack of evidence to rebuff U.S. accusations against former Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha, who was indicted by the U.S. earlier this year on charges that he aided the Sinaloa cartel in exchange for bribes and political backing. Although Sheinbaum forced Rocha to resign, she has consistently rejected a U.S. request for his extradition.
 “Let’s be clear: First they come for some, then for others, until offices of the Department of Justice decide elections in Mexico,” she said at a rally earlier this year.
 Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit said last week that it blocked bank accounts of firms and individuals sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury as a preventive measure after detecting “risky financial transactions and irregularities reported by financial institutions.” It made no reference about alleged links of these individuals to organized crime. A spokesman for the unit declined to comment.
 The U.S. Treasury described Ávila’s ex-husband, Carlos Torres, as a cartel-linked political operator who has an alliance with a Sinaloa cartel boss operating in the border city of Mexicali. “Torres uses his political influence to facilitate cartel activities and protect the Sinaloa Cartel from government and law-enforcement intervention in Baja California,” the U.S. Treasury said on Monday.

 IMF Chief tells economic leaders: the time to act is now
 Fabiana Negrin Ochoa , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 7 Oct 2026, 05:05 PM IST 
 Summary
 Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said the global economy is caught in a tug of war between an energy shock and an artificial-intelligence boom. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The global economy is caught in a tug of war between an energy shock and an artificial-intelligence boom.
 Those forces are testing the resilience economies have shown through a series of crises, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday.
 Mounting global public debt—on track to exceed 100% of gross domestic product—adds a third source of pressure, she said Wednesday.
 In a curtain-raiser speech in Singapore ahead of next week’s IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, she identified those three factors as central to discussions among finance ministers and central bank governors gathering in the Thai capital.
 “Whether the world’s underwhelming growth rates this decade can be bettered will depend on our success in navigating three major crosscurrents: the rapid arrival of AI, persistently high energy prices, and record levels of public debt,” she said.
 The meetings come against a backdrop of high uncertainty and rapid change.
 A longer-than-expected energy crisis caused by the Middle East conflict is fueling inflation, adding another supply shock while disruptions from the Ukraine war linger. That has forced many central banks to raise interest rates and stoked expectations of further increases.
 Tightening financial conditions have amplified concerns about the fiscal health of advanced economies such as the U.S., sending bond yields to multiyear highs—one of the clearest alarm bells markets can ring.
 “Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defense,” Georgieva said.
 For now, measures such as diversifying fuel sources and tapping strategic reserves have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Iran crisis. But the recovery in Gulf flows remains shaky, and oil is still around $100 barrel, Georgieva said.
 “Factor in the structural global shortfall in refining capacity, and we get retail prices of diesel and other refined products at record highs,” she added.
 Natural-gas supplies from the Gulf remain severely disrupted—hitting Asia and Europe particularly hard.
 Indicators such as purchasing managers surveys suggest manufacturers are weathering the shock relatively well. But businesses can absorb only so much pressure on margins as energy and other input costs keep rising. Many firms have started passing on those costs to consumers, broadening inflationary pressures for which there is no easy fix.
 “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” Georgieva said, noting that Brent futures point to expensive oil through 2027.
 As energy prices push up inflation, policy rates and benchmark bond yields are rising too. U.S., German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields are at their highest levels since 2007, 2009 and 1996, respectively, and still climbing, she noted.
 Excessive fiscal deficits and high debt-servicing costs suggest many that now is a good time for many central banks to tilt hawkish, she said, calling it “highly appropriate” that the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan have all raised rates and spoken firmly.
 AI has been a major source of economic resilience.
 “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” the IMF chief said.
 But that growth engine carries risks.
 Power-hungry AI adds to energy demand, while the AI building boom itself is inflationary, Georgieva said.
 Growing economic and financial concentration in the technology poses another risk.
 If AI-centric earnings fall short of expectations, hyperscalers’ leverage and large global holdings of U.S. equities could turn disappointment into a far-reaching shock, she said.
 The first line of defense, Georgieva said, is regulation and supervision.
 Experts have also warned that frontier AI models could disrupt the financial system on which the world economy relies. Leading developer Anthropic called on AI labs to slow down, while OpenAI scrapped the release of its next-generation model over safety concerns.
 On fiscal policy—“the place where all pressures meet”—Georgieva urged advanced economies with high debt to act decisively on credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, including measures to ease pressure on monetary policy.
 “Putting all of it together, my message to the world’s economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action—you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.”

docs.title: TCS Q2 earnings: Five things to watch as Tata boardroom fight adds to scrutiny
docs.text:

 TCS Q2 earnings: Five things to watch as Tata boardroom fight adds to scrutiny
 Jas Bardia 5 min read 7 Oct 2026, 08:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 TCS’s second-quarter results will offer clues on demand, AI revenue, data-centre spending and margins, while investors assess whether the Tata Sons dispute could distract its top leadership. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Mumbai: Tata Consultancy Services Ltd (TCS) will report its fiscal second-quarter results on Thursday with an unusual distraction: a boardroom fight at its parent over the man who once ran it.
 On 17 September, the Tata Sons board gave chairman N. Chandrasekaran a third five-year term, despite opposition from Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata. The dispute has raised questions over the validity of the board’s decisions—and over whether the battle at the parent could distract the group’s most important profit engine. Dividends from TCS, the crown jewel of the group, accounted for 88.5% of Tata Sons’ ₹ 31,961 crore profit in fiscal year 2026 (FY26).
 TCS has faced difficulties for two years. Last year, it recorded its first full-year revenue decline since it went public in 2004. Chandrasekaran, who was TCS’s chief executive for almost eight years until 2017, has since become more involved in decisions at the company. His increasing influence is now a topic of discussion among senior TCS leaders.
 The feud at the parent has not hurt client relationships, but employees question whether it could distract senior leadership, Chandrasekaran included.
 His imprint on TCS’s recent strategy is clear. He approved the company’s entry into data centres in November last year, with plans to set up a 1 gigawatt (GW) facility worth $6.5 billion. He also backed the appointments of Mangesh Sathe as chief strategy officer and Aarthi Subramanian as chief operating officer.
 Sathe has since been instrumental in setting up the company’s unit overseeing global capability centres ( GCCs ), while Subramanian runs weekly reviews with TCS leaders on business needs and artificial intelligence (AI) strategy.
 So when TCS reports its second-quarter report card on Thursday, scrutiny will fall on Chandrasekaran as well as chief executive K. Krithivasan. Here are five things to watch when TCS declares its second-quarter earnings on 8 October.
 Revenue sets the tone 
 The second quarter (July-September) is typically TCS’s strongest season, and it matters for two reasons. It sets the tone for peers reporting next week and largely determines how TCS’s year ends, as furloughs and holidays shrink billing days and imply weaker growth in the second half.
 At least three brokerages expect constant-currency (CC) growth of 0.4-0.6%, driven by banking and manufacturing clients.
 “We estimate revenue growth of 0.6% q-o-q (quarter-on-quarter) CC in Q2FY27, led by healthy deal ramp-up in Jul'26/Aug'26, partly offset by delays in TCV to revenue conversion in Sep'26. TCS is seeing recovery in its manufacturing vertical, but softness in retail and CMT continues,” ICICI Securities analysts Richa Mukhija, Aditi Patil and Seema Nayak wrote in a 27 September note.
 The company ended the April-June quarter (Q1FY27) with revenue of $7.62 billion, flat sequentially and up 2.7% from a year earlier.
 Demand is the bigger signal 
 TCS’s view on demand will shape expectations for the entire sector.
 Last week, Accenture Plc described a changing demand situation, mostly the same as last year. Investors will watch for signs that the conflict in West Asia is prompting clients to cut optional tech spending and focus on core operations.
 AI faces a harder test 
 The company’s commentary on artificial intelligence (AI) will be closely tracked, as it is one of the few tech services firms to report AI revenue. Annualized AI revenue rose 13.6% sequentially to $2.6 billion last quarter.
 The impact of token costs on clients’ AI budgets and revenue-productivity asks will also be closely watched.
 According to experts, most new renewals come with a 35% productivity ask upfront, which is further expected to hurt revenue. Against this backdrop, TCS’s ability to win new work and offset revenue deflation will be closely watched. The company’s rate card for AI work will also be tracked.
 “Annualized AI services revenue should continue the strong momentum (+13.6% QoQ in 1Q) due to increasing demand for AI-led modernization, autonomous GBS, cybersecurity, and sovereign cloud,” Motilal Oswal Financial Services analysts Abhishek Pathak, Keval Bhagat and Suket Kothari wrote in a 1 October note.
 Data centres are a new variable 
 TCS was the first big information technology (IT) services company to enter data centres.
 Last month, it said it had acquired 264 acres in Hyderabad for an AI data centre campus of up to 1GW. The company has invested about ₹ 200 crore in the unit, HyperVault, so far, according to its yearly reports. Investors will watch spending plans and progress.
 Margins face twin pressures 
 Profit margins face pressure from two sides. AI is making competition tougher between large and mid-sized IT firms, and TCS may need to lower prices to win big deals. Data centres require heavy investment and could reduce profits.
 “We forecast a 100 bps y-o-y (year-on-year) margin decline and stable qoq margins. The yoy decline reflects wage revisions, the impact of acquisitions, and ongoing pricing pressure. Ebit margins typically expand in the quarter following annual wage hikes, supporting sequential stability,” Kotak Institutional Equities analysts Kawaljeet Saluja, Sathishkumar S. and Vamshi Krishna wrote in a 28 September note.

 A High-Stakes Gambit Clinched Paramount’s Warner Deal
 Joe Flint , The Wall Street Journal 6 min read 7 Oct 2026, 06:06 PM IST 
 Summary
 David Ellison’s megadeal combining Paramount and Warner Bros. closed Tuesday, ushering in a new era for Hollywood. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 David Ellison was on the ropes.
 It was late July, and a judge had handed down a temporary restraining order halting the media mogul’s $81 billion deal to combine his Paramount entertainment company with the much larger Warner Bros. Discovery—an early setback in his antitrust battle with 12 state attorneys general.
 Faced with a choice between going straight to trial or stepping into another short-term skirmish to avoid a preliminary injunction, Ellison, 43, took the big gamble.
 He would see the states, led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, in court.
 Rather than spend months fighting over whether the merger should remain frozen while the case proceeded, Paramount agreed to keep the companies apart and pushed to get directly to a trial on the merits.
 It was a risky gambit. A loss at trial could kill the deal, and a lengthy legal journey would prove expensive as Paramount was set to rack up hefty fees it had agreed to pay Warner shareholders if the merger was delayed.
 But over the following weeks, Ellison waged a concerted behind-the-scenes campaign, people familiar with the matter said.
 He crisscrossed the country courting politicians, hired well-connected operatives and lobbyists to work regulators and lawmakers, cultivated allies with Republicans and Democrats and, in a pivotal move, even threatened to move his empire out of California.
 California’s Gavin Newsom publicly called on the two sides to settle the matter, and privately encouraged the attorney general to go to the table. Ellison met with Newsom on more than one occasion, the people familiar with the matter said.
 Ellison’s efforts all came to fruition on Tuesday when Paramount officially closed the Warner deal and met with employees of the combined company—now renamed Skydance—at a town hall on the Warner Bros. studio lot.
 “Now let’s be honest. It wasn’t easy to get here,” Ellison said, according to a transcript viewed by The Wall Street Journal. “At times it was downright ugly. And at nearly every turn, someone told us it couldn’t be done. And here we are.”
 “I’d do it all over again in a heartbeat,” he added.
 Ellison is now responsible for some of the biggest brands and franchises in show business, including movie and television studios with historic filmmaking lots, plus two streaming services in Paramount+ and HBO Max and dozens of cable channels. His decisions will determine the fates of Batman, Superman, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Harry Potter, CNN, CBS News and other properties.
 He’s wasted little time putting his team in charge, this week announcing a flurry of executive appointments to lead streaming strategy, movie studios and TV programming operations. So far his biggest hiring move has been recruiting former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz to be co-CEO. Skydance on Tuesday said Emerson Collective founder Laurene Powell Jobs and Activision founder Bobby Kotick will join the board.
 The combined media giant will close with nearly $80 billion in debt, which analysts have said could weigh on Ellison’s ambitions to create a Hollywood powerhouse. Layoffs are expected, as Ellison has promised $6 billion in annual synergies within three years.
 Tuesday’s victory lap was the culmination of what Ellison described in his remarks as a long-term plan that was three years in the making.
 After a grueling process, he secured control of Paramount in August 2025, merging it with his Skydance Media production company. By then, the idea had already come to Ellison to pursue Warner Bros.
 Warner Bros. was once the gold standard for Hollywood—both on the big screen and behind the scenes. Now, it’s being sold for the third time in a decade. Photo: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
 Warner Chief Executive David Zaslav passed on Ellison’s first few offers, which started at $19 a share. But Ellison persisted and Warner put itself up for auction. Netflix soon swooped in and signed a deal to acquire the movie and TV studios and HBO Max streaming service.
 Ellison refused to back down, sweetening his offers, taking his bid directly to shareholders and threatening a proxy fight while enlisting Trump allies to lobby on his behalf.
 On his ninth offer, Ellison prevailed. Paramount agreed to pay $81 billion for Warner after Netflix declined to match an offer that was 63% higher than Ellison’s first.
 Next, Ellison had to get the deal through regulators here and abroad.
 That task fell primarily to chief legal officer Makan Delrahim, one of Ellison’s first hires after acquiring Paramount. Ellison set up a war room on the Paramount lot where he, Delrahim and one or two other executives would meet daily to map out strategy and measure progress, said one of the people familiar with the matter.
 A former Trump administration antitrust chief, Delrahim was intimately familiar with Warner. As head of the Justice Department’s antitrust division, he led the government’s ultimately unsuccessful effort to block AT&T’s acquisition of what was then called Time Warner in 2018.
 One of Delrahim’s first moves was to tap Jon Leibowitz, who chaired the Federal Trade Commission under President Barack Obama, as an outside antitrust adviser.
 Getting approval from the Justice Department came with relative ease, as did approvals from the European Union, United Kingdom, China and other regions.
 But a hurdle emerged when California’s Bonta, joined by 11 other states, including New York, Connecticut and Colorado, sued to block the merger on antitrust grounds. The states alleged that the deal would illegally consolidate markets including those for theatrical films and

 Listen to This Article
 Disclaimer: This article is written by Ajit Mishra, SVP-Research at Religare Broking. Views expressed are his own. Readers' discretion is advised. 
 Markets reversed the recent gains on Wednesday and ended lower amid volatility, weighed down by a combination of domestic and global factors. After a weak opening and an initial recovery attempt, the benchmark indices failed to sustain their gains and oscillated within a narrow range. The Nifty closed at 22,603.05, down 0.76 per cent, while the Sensex settled at 72,638.70, lower by 0.59 per cent.
 On the sectoral front, metal remained the key drag, followed by realty and auto, while banking and media ended with modest gains. Meanwhile, the broader indices traded mixed, with the midcap index declining 0.63 per cent, while the smallcap index gained 0.30 per cent.
 The overall market tone remained neutral following the RBI’s widely anticipated 25-bps repo rate hike to 5.5 per cent, with the stronger growth outlook initially supporting rate-sensitive sectors like banking. However, sentiment softened as investors weighed the higher inflation outlook and shift to a calibrated tightening stance, keeping the broader market mood cautious. Global macro concerns added to the pressure, with Brent crude rebounding above $101 a barrel, while continued foreign outflows, elevated global bond yields and rupee weakness remained key overhangs for domestic equities.
 Technically, the Nifty’s inability to cross the 22,800 zone reaffirms the prevailing cautious undertone in the near-term setup. The 22,500 remains the immediate support, followed by the 22,400-22,200 level, while 22,800–23,000 is likely to act as the key resistance zone. For now, a selective and hedged approach remains suitable, with a preference for stock-specific opportunities rather than aggressive index-level exposure.

 Illustration: Binay Sinha

 Listen to This Article
 India’s capital markets are languishing under multiple headwinds, even as stocks tied to the financial-market ecosystem continue to enjoy strong investor appetite. 
 At a time when portfolios are bleeding as the Nifty 50 has lost nearly 13 per cent on a year-to-date (YTD) basis, the Nifty Capital Markets, a 17-stock index constituting brokers, asset managers and market infrastructure plays, has rallied 13 per cent during the same period, signalling strong appetite for these companies. 
 However, the gains are not even. Ten of 17 stocks rose during the period, with Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) leading the way with a 49 per cent gain. Anand Rathi Wealth follows suit on the back of a 38 per cent rise. Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL), Angel One, BSE, Aditya Birla Sun Life AMC and Nuvama Wealth Management are among other top gainers with a 24-26 per cent increase.

 Cumulatively, these 17 stocks have added ₹1.22 trillion to investors' wealth so far in 2026.
 Explaining the traction in these companies, Harshal Dasani, business head at INVAsset, called them the "toll roads" for the equity market. "They earn on turnover and assets under management, not on whether the index rises. A correction with high volatility is good for turnover, and a correction absorbed by domestic flows is good for AUM. Both have happened at once," Dasani said.
 Even as foreign investors have offloaded stocks worth crores, the domestic faith in equities has largely stayed put as signalled by the SIP numbers. So far in FY27 (as of August), SIP contribution is at ₹1.58 trillion, with inflows of over ₹30,000 crore in all five months of the fiscal. In FY26, the figure was ₹3.49 trillion. Every rupee passes through this index's constituents regardless of where the Nifty settles.
 The number of NSE active investors has seen a healthy 26 per cent CAGR over FY20-26, with the mix of participation shifting meaningfully toward derivatives and cross-segment trading, said Macquarie in a note in September. Additionally, it said, SIP contribution has become an increasingly important and stable pillar of mutual fund AUM.
 The earnings trajectory confirms this trend. BSE, for instance, reported a 62 per cent jump in consolidated net profit to ₹872.66 crore in Q1FY27, while Groww reported a 94 per cent increase. Anand Rathi Wealth saw a healthy 24 per cent increase, Nuvama Wealth 16 per cent and MOFSL 10 per cent. Check - TOP GAINERS NSE | TOP LOSERS NSE 
 Outlook: Capital market stocks
 With the growing financialisation trend, analysts at Macquarie said brokers and exchanges should benefit from a larger investor base, rising engagement and broader monetisation across investment products. 
 Indians save $500 billion annually in financial assets, and almost 50 per cent is parked in cash and deposits. This pool is ready for market-linked products, which will drive a 16 per cent CAGR in India’s combined investment & wealth and exchanges revenue pool over FY26-30E, estimates the global brokerage. 
 "Though regulations may disrupt volumes, historically we have seen volume recovery on the back of stronger investor protection, transparency and market stability, thereby strengthening the market," it said.
 Dasani, too, expects traction in these companies but the trend will not be uniform. The AUM-linked businesses, asset managers and depositories, have the most durable earnings because SIP money is contractual and sticky, and that part of the index should hold through an ordinary correction, he said. 
 The turnover-linked businesses, he said, face two risks the current prices do not fully carry. The first is regulation: cash turnover already dipped and F&O growth was sluggish in FY26 after the derivatives curbs; the second is reflexivity: a 14 per cent Nifty drawdown without retail capitulation is the base case so far, but a deeper fall that raises SIP stoppages would hit turnover and AUM at the same time.
 But a recent Phillip Capital note reinforces its bullishness on the broking industry. It initiated coverage on Groww and Anand Rathi with 'Buy' ratings in a September 30 report as it expects these two names to be best positioned to capture the industry's structural shift from transaction-led brokerage to a diversified, recurring-revenue financial-platform model.

FPIs rotate out of rate-sensitive sectors amid high interest rates
 Financials see sharpest outflows as investors favour pharma, consumer services
 Financial services recorded the sharpest FPI outflows during the month, with investors selling shares worth ₹13,147 crore, compared with inflows of ₹10,494 crore in the previous month. (Illustration: Binay Sinha)
 Kairavi Lukka Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 08 2026 | 7:37 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Overseas investors turned net sellers of Indian equities in September, offloading shares worth ₹35,861 crore and ending a two-month buying streak in July and August, according to data from the National Securities Depository. They had bought ₹29,631 crore worth of shares in August.
 Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) shifted their preferences during the month, moving away from interest rate-sensitive sectors such as banking, automotive, and oil and gas. Of the 24 sectors tracked, nine recorded inflows in September, while 14 saw outflows. The healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors recorded inflows, although domestic institutions accounted for a larger share of the buying than foreign institutional investors (FIIs).
 Financial services recorded the sharpest FPI outflows during the month, with investors selling shares worth ₹13,147 crore, compared with inflows of ₹10,494 crore in August. This was followed by net selling of ₹3,000-6,900 crore in fast-moving consumer goods, metals and mining, telecommunications, automotive and automotive components, and oil, gas and consumable fuels. In contrast, consumer services attracted the highest inflows in September, at ₹2,333 crore. 
 A report from SBI Securities said that amid global macroeconomic challenges in 2026, including high global interest rates, geopolitical tensions, and rupee volatility, foreign investors might be treating consumer services as a defensive buffer.

 “India’s expanding middle-class demographic continues to drive strong growth in discretionary spending,” the report said. “Segments such as travel and tourism, hospitality and food services, retail and ecommerce remain highly underpenetrated compared with developed markets, presenting long-term opportunities that institutional capital seeks.”
 Healthcare and pharmaceutical are generally considered defensive sectors because demand for medicines tends to be relatively inelastic, even during periods of high inflation or economic uncertainty. This defensive nature can also support higher price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples.
 Over the past two months, as oil prices have risen and interest rates have remained high, institutional investors have increased their exposure to relatively expensive sectors such as pharmaceutical. They have been selling public-sector banks, which trade at around 7x earnings, oil and gas companies at around 11x and metals at around 17x, while buying pharmaceutical stocks, where the average P/E multiple is around 41x.
 SBI Securities said the sector recorded net cumulative FII inflows of ₹2,117 crore in September 2026, following more than ₹13,600 crore of inflows over the previous two months, indicating sustained buying interest.
 “The three months of consistent buying comes after a prolonged phase of sustained outflows from April 2025 to June this year, suggesting a gradual shift in investor positioning towards the sector,” it said.
 Sectoral trends also changed between the first and second halves of September. Compared with the first half of the month, FPIs bought more equities in consumer services and textile and turned buyers from sellers in real estate. However, selling intensified in several sectors, including metals and mining, telecommunications, automotive and automotive components, oil, gas and consumable fuels, financial services, construction material, capital goods, and consumer durables.

Rising fuel costs, margin fears put cement stocks on a weak foundation
 Cement demand is likely to improve, but higher fuel, packaging and logistics costs could weigh on margins and delay earnings upgrades until the fourth quarter of FY27
 premium 
 Prices declined slightly in July–August 2026 and recovered in September, with increases sustained by demand
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 11:36 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Cement volumes are estimated to have grown by 6–7 per cent year-on-year in Q2FY27, and some companies such as Shree Cement , JK Cement and UltraTech may have improved their market share. Realisations may also have improved by 1–2 per cent quarter-on-quarter, due to price increases in August and September. But higher crude prices and higher petcoke prices present challenges. Rising raw material and logistics costs hurt margins, and earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) may fall appreciably quarter-on-quarter.
 Volume growth in a seasonally weak quarter was a positive surprise. Prices declined slightly in July–August 2026 and recovered in September, with increases sustained by demand. Ebitda per tonne will fall sequentially as well as year-on-year for most companies.
 Imported petcoke prices have risen by 30–35 per cent quarter-on-quarter, and this may also affect Q3FY27 costs, given long-term inventory. Thermal coal prices also rose 1–2 per cent quarter-on-quarter. Packaging costs have also risen due to the impact of high crude oil and gas prices.
 Volumes should grow in H2FY27, and price increases could be sustained, given busy-season demand. Pricing picked up across regions in September, and more increases may be implemented in Q3 if demand recovery is visible. But analysts are concerned about rural demand tapering due to an erratic monsoon. Construction activity in Q3 will be moderated by the festive season and by pollution-related bans in North India.
 Margin compression could continue until there’s a resolution to the conflict in West Asia. Fuel (crude and coal) costs can be visible with a long lag of three months or more. Cement spreads (realisations net of fuel and freight costs) indicate a significant decline in margins. Companies with longer inventory cycles may see the impact of high Q2FY27 fuel costs on their financials through Q3FY27. ALSO READ: PVR Inox rallies 10%; stock hits 22-month high in weak market 
 Pricing discipline will be crucial until demand recovery is clearly visible. It is tempting for companies with surplus capacity to start a price war, but this would hurt the industry. Rural demand may be uneven given monsoon patterns, but government-budgeted infrastructure spending, with execution across roads, railways and metros, and some private corporate capex could keep demand ticking over. The Index of Industrial Production (IIP) trends indicate double-digit year-on-year growth in cement output through July–August. Overall FY27 demand is expected to grow by 7–8 per cent year-on-year, which is supported by the trend in Q2 volumes. In the longer term, the industry is assumed to see steady annual volume growth of 6–8 per cent during FY27–FY29. 
 The sustainability of recent price increases would be critical if inflationary price trends affect the industry through Q3FY27. Dealer inventory and non-trade demand are other factors to monitor, along with regional differences in demand and pricing.
 Maintaining margins will be challenging, although a pickup in demand is likely. The industry has surplus capacity, which is growing given the expansion plans of all major players. Earnings upgrades will be gradual in H2 and may not be seen until Q4FY27, unless tensions in West Asia ease.
 The long-term structural narrative is simple. India is growing at a reasonable pace, and government spending on infrastructure is a big part of the story, with investments across infrastructure, urban development and logistics, and policy incentives for manufacturing and affordable housing. Areas like data centres, renewables and uptake of production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes for manufacturing should drive private sector capex. All this will sustain cement demand.
 Within the industry, consolidation has been a theme for two to three years, and it is continuing. This should improve pricing discipline. Most players are also investing in renewables, waste heat recovery systems (WHRS) and alternative fuels, and improving operational efficiencies. These are cost-saving initiatives that should push up margins as and when input cost pressures ease. Scale is a must to exploit rising demand and also to lower operational costs per tonne, and capex has been ongoing.
 However, this story and the positive outlook will only play out over the medium to long term. In the near term, earnings are being dragged down by high fuel costs, which are dependent on geopolitical tensions and thus unpredictable.
 Some investors have started to experience fatigue since they have been holding cement exposures for a long period without receiving much in the way of returns. A lack of share price appreciation has also led to corrections, which may make valuations more attractive.
 The factors that investors should look for are relatively easy to identify. A pan-India market presence is a must. Higher exposure to infrastructure is useful. Efficient internal cost optimisation and scale are mandatory. This means the induction of renewables and WHRS. Domestic coal and coke linkages are a big bonus. Strong balance sheets with low debt will help in funding expansions. Few companies check all the boxes.

docs.title: Nuvama initiates coverage on RR Kabel with ‘Buy’: Sees 20% upside on export surge
docs.text: Multiple structural tailwinds are supporting the domestic cables and wires (C&W) industry. These include increasing renewable energy capacity, accelerating transmission and distribution spending, and expansion in data centre capacity among others. India’s third largest player in this segment, RR Kabel, well positioned to capitalise on the growing demand opportunity, particularly in cables. Brokerage house Nuvama Institutional Equities has initiated coverage on the stock with a ‘Buy’ rating and has set a target price of Rs 3,310 apiece, implying a 20% upside from the stock’s current level. Nuvama on RR Kabel: Cables as new growth engine The company is expanding its cable portfolio from 66 kilovolt to 220 kilovolt through a Rs 1,000 crore capital expenditure plan during FY25 to FY28. Nuvama expects more capacity additions in the future. ALSO READ5 investment themes, 20 stocks: How to ride India’s next capex boom “This will enable the company to enter the higher-voltage cable segment, benefiting from strong domestic demand and growing export opportunities, while expanding its addressable market and market share,” Nuvama said. Nuvama on RR Kabel: Growing exports The company has built a strong export network, which contributed 21-30% of its C&W revenue during FY19 to FY26. RR Kabel has a well-diversified presence across Europe and the Middle East. The company also continues to expand its footprint in the US to reduce dependence on the Middle East amid the ongoing war. “As increasing competition and large capacity additions by leading industry players and incumbents raise the risk of domestic overcapacity, RR Kabel's established export presence positions it well to diversify demand and sustain growth through international markets,” Nuvama said. Nuvama on RR Kabel: Margin expansion, FMEG turnaround RR Kabel continues to improve profitability in its core C&W business, with the earnings before interest and tax margin expanding to 8.9% in FY26 and 9.9% in Q1 FY27 from 7.5% in FY19. This growth is driven by pricing actions, operating leverage, and sustained cost optimisation. Moreover, breakeven is expected in the fast-moving electrical goods segment by FY28. This segment is supported by premiumisation, improved product mix, and better realisation. Nuvama believes RR Kabel is significantly exposed to the impending heightened competitive intensity in the domestic wires segment. “This will drive pricing intensity along with increased spending (employee cost, inventory carrying cost, A&P spends) in order to protect market share. However, this will be more than offset by i) better mix (higher cables and exports mix) and ii) operating leverage, in our opinion,” the brokerage said. ALSO READNomura initiates coverage on this optical cable play: Datacentre capex to fuel 35% rally? Nuvama on RR Kabel: Good play in C&W segment Nuvama believes RR Kabel can capitalise on the growing real-estate led wires growth opportunity. The company’s substantial export presence is well placed to navigate any near term headwinds from intense competition. The brokerage is bullish on the stock and has projected an upside of 20% from current levels. docs.title: HDFC Bank down 29% this year: Is it a ‘Buy’ now as Anup Bagchi takes charge?
docs.text: India’s largest private lender, HDFC Bank, has had a tumultuous year so far. The sudden resignation of former part-time chairman Atanu Chakraborty was seen as the beginning of the troubles as investors became apprehensive about the lender’s management. In fact, the HDFC Bank share price has been seen in doldrums for several months now. The stock has lost nearly 29% this year so far. On September 11, the HDFC Bank share price hit a 31-month low of Rs 681.90 apiece. HDFC Bank: Opportunity to reset? However, Financialexpress.com spoke to several experts who see this as ‘an opportunity to reset’ for the banking major. Can the appointment of Anup Bagchi as the MD and CEO, which was announced last week, change the bank’s fortunes? Is it the right time to buy? Kotak Securities remains constructive on the bank after the appointment of Bagchi. “The transition provides an opportunity to reset strategy, with greater focus on profitability, liability franchise and improving return ratios. Bagchi's track record in franchise building and execution is a positive,” said Shrikant Chouhan, Head Equity Research at Kotak Securities. HDFC Bank: Bagchi’s appointment clears near-term hurdles Chouhan said the important factor to take note is that the negative sentiment around the bank “appears” to be out and is now being addressed through the leadership change and strategic reset. He added that valuations are attractive, signalling a good entry opportunity. ALSO READ3 Top Pharma CDMO Stocks in India to Add to Your Watchlist Following the appointment of Bagchi, global brokerage house Nomura said it removes any uncertainty around management succession and the focus will now shift to Bagchi’s strategic priorities and execution plans. Bagchi’s experience across retail and wholesale banking, capital markets, digital banking, and insurance provides a broad operating background to steer the bank through its next phase of growth. “While the external appointment provides an opportunity for a strategic reset, the pace of execution and clarity on the medium-term growth strategy will be critical for investor confidence and a sustained re-rating,” Nomura had said. Sneha Poddar, VP-Research, Wealth Management, at Motilal Oswal Financial Services said, “HDFC Bank is undergoing management transition after a series of adverse developments, challenges in operating performance after its merger with HDFC Ltd, and significant erosion of shareholder wealth over recent years.” Poddar added that Bagchi brings over three decades of experience and this removes a “key overhang” surrounding the leadership succession and provides an external perspective at a time when the bank is seeking to rebuild investor confidence. “A new leadership team, alongside an improvement in growth and earnings trajectory, should improve investor sentiment.” HDFC Bank: Is it time to buy? Japanese brokerage major, Nomura has also retained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and its target price is at Rs 950. This implies a 35% upside from the stock’s current price of Rs 702.5 apiece. Other brokerages that have a ‘Buy’ recommendation on the stock include Jefferies, Motilal Oswal, Emkay Global, PL Capital, and Axis Securities. Sameer Sawant, research analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan believes this is an “opportune” time to buy HDFC Bank. The stock has underperformed the bank index meaningfully, and the focus in the near term will stay on improving the liability mix before growth picks up. Core deposit growth is already running ahead of advances and asset quality remains stable, Sawant said. All eyes are now on the growth trajectory that the bank outlines during its Q2 earnings announcement.
